title: Mandatory Helmets in a Himalayan Village
scenario: District transport officer Tenzin Dorji in Bhutan is asked by the ministry to enforce a new rule requiring helmets on all motorbikes in the mountain town of Trashigang. Local elders and monks argue that traditional headwear and short village journeys make the rule unnecessary. Hospital records show a rising number of head injuries, mostly among young men. Fines would hit poor families hard. Tenzin must decide how to implement the rule.
options: Enforce the rule firmly with fines from the start, giving priority to preventing head injuries.
Run a three-month education and free-helmet scheme first, with enforcement delayed until awareness grows.
Enforce on main roads and highways only and exempt short village lanes, recognising local conditions.
tension: public health vs. liberty and custom

title: Closing the Beach After a Shark Sighting
scenario: Mayor Lorena Castillo of a small Pacific resort town in Costa Rica must decide whether to ban swimming for a week after a bull shark bit a tourist. Hotels, surf schools and street vendors earn most of their income in this season. A marine biologist says the risk is low but real, and bans rarely stop determined swimmers. Residents have always swum there. Lorena must decide how to respond.
options: Close the beach to swimming for the week, enforcing it with lifeguards and fines, to prevent another attack.
Keep the beach open with warning flags and extra lifeguards, leaving swimmers to decide for themselves.
Close the beach for three days while a survey is carried out, then reopen on the findings.

title: Compulsory Evacuation of the Stubborn Fisherman
scenario: Cyclone warning officer Rubina Akter in Cox's Bazar must decide whether police may physically remove people from a coastal embankment settlement that is under a mandatory evacuation order. An old fisherman, Jalil, refuses to leave his boat and hut, saying he survived worse storms and that looters took everything last time. His neighbours say he will drown. Forcing him would be traumatic; leaving him may cost his life and endanger rescuers later. Rubina must decide.
options: Authorise police to remove him by force, since the storm is predicted to be severe and he may drown.
Respect his refusal, document it, and leave him with a radio and an offer of transport until the last minute.
Arrange for a neighbour or relative he trusts to guard the boat so that he agrees to leave voluntarily.

title: Smoking Ban in the Housing Block
scenario: Housing association manager Brigid Gallagher in Cork has learned that a tenant, a man in his seventies on oxygen therapy, keeps smoking on his balcony where flammable canisters are stored. A fire there could endanger a block of 60 flats. A ban on smoking in the tenancy agreement exists but evicting an elderly tenant would effectively leave him homeless. Neighbours are complaining. Brigid must decide how to enforce the safety rule.
options: Issue a formal eviction notice, enforcing the rule to protect all residents.
Offer him alternative arrangements, such as a ground-floor flat or supervised smoking area, and enforce only if he refuses.
Remove the oxygen canisters from his balcony and leave smoking alone, treating the oxygen as the main hazard.

title: Contact Tracing App and the Shared Phone
scenario: Public health data lead Dr. Thandi Moyo in Bulawayo is designing a mandatory contact tracing requirement for markets during a fast-moving outbreak. Many market traders share a single phone or have none, and the system would require registering a phone number to enter. Without the rule, officials say tracing becomes impossible. With it, poorer traders will be shut out of work. She must recommend the rule's form.
options: Recommend mandatory phone registration for all market entry, accepting that some will be excluded.
Recommend paper sign-in sheets at the gates for those without phones, even though they are slower and less reliable.
Recommend voluntary registration with incentives such as free masks, accepting lower coverage in exchange for fairness.
tension: public health surveillance vs. access and livelihoods

title: Banning Fireworks on a Festival Night
scenario: City councillor Dang Thi Hoa in Hue is asked to propose a ban on private fireworks for the Lunar New Year after an increase in burns and a fire that damaged an old wooden house. Many families see fireworks as essential to the holiday and to warding off bad luck. A licensed public display is proposed as a replacement. Compliance is uncertain and the black market is active. Hoa must decide what to recommend.
options: Recommend a full ban on private fireworks, with an official display as the sole alternative.
Recommend a licence system permitting small, low-risk fireworks in designated open areas only.
Recommend no ban but a safety campaign and stricter penalties for damage or injury, treating the custom as protected.

title: Lockdown Rules and the Dying Grandmother
scenario: Police constable Aroha Ngata in Auckland is posted at a checkpoint during a strict regional lockdown. A man, Hemi, asks to cross to see his grandmother, who is dying in a care home on the other side and who has been asking for him. Rules allow only immediate family visits with documented permission, which takes days. Hemi is not immediate family under the rule, though in his culture the grandmother raised him. Aroha must decide whether to let him through.
options: Refuse him, applying the rule consistently, since exceptions could undermine compliance and put others at risk.
Let him through with a mask and a promise of testing afterwards, judging that the rule should yield to compassion.
Phone her sergeant to request an emergency exception and keep Hemi waiting at the checkpoint until a decision comes.

title: Mandatory Seatbelts for Taxi Passengers
scenario: Road safety commissioner Dr. Amara Kone in Abidjan is considering rules that would make rear seatbelts compulsory for all taxi passengers, with fines for drivers. Many shared taxis carry five or six people in a space meant for four, so belts cannot be fitted for everyone, and the rule could price poor commuters off the road. Fatality figures show high deaths among rear passengers. Amara must decide whether to recommend the rule.
options: Recommend the mandatory rule, with a phase-in period for retrofitting vehicles and capped fares.
Recommend limiting passenger numbers to the number of seatbelts, even though that reduces transport capacity.
Recommend an awareness campaign and voluntary standards for now, fearing the rule would harm commuters.

title: The Bonfire Ban in a Dry Summer
scenario: Fire marshal Konstantinos Papadakis on the Greek island of Chios must decide whether to ban the traditional village bonfire at a saint's feast after weeks without rain. The bonfire has been held for centuries and the community says that cancelling it would break faith with the dead. Wind forecasts suggest a modest but real chance of embers lighting dry scrub on a slope above the houses. Konstantinos must decide.
options: Ban the bonfire outright for this year, citing the extreme fire risk.
Allow a smaller bonfire in the paved square with water tankers and fire crews on standby.
Allow the bonfire as usual with volunteers on watch, trusting the community's long experience.
tension: safety vs. tradition and cultural liberty

title: Raising the Drinking Age During an Outbreak
scenario: Health minister's adviser Ricardo Alves in Maputo is asked whether to close nightclubs and ban alcohol sales in the capital for two weeks to curb a surge in road deaths and assaults over the holiday. Venue owners and workers, many informally employed, would lose earnings with no safety net. Evidence that closures would reduce deaths is plausible but not conclusive. Ricardo must recommend a course.
options: Recommend the closures and sales ban, giving priority to protecting lives over the economic loss.
Recommend shorter hours and stricter enforcement against drunk driving instead of a full closure.
Recommend no closures but a targeted compensation fund and a campaign for safe transport home.

title: Leash Law After the Dog Attack
scenario: After a stray-dog attack on a child, municipal council member Oksana Melnyk in Lviv proposes a rule requiring all dogs to be leashed and muzzled in parks, along with mandatory registration. Owners argue that their well-trained dogs would suffer and that the rule will push people to abandon pets. Animal shelters are full already. Oksana must decide how strict her proposal should be.
options: Propose strict leashing, muzzling and registration for all dogs, prioritising child safety.
Propose rules only for breeds with a recorded record of attacks, leaving other owners free.
Propose enforcement of existing owner liability laws with higher fines, and leash rules only in playgrounds.

title: Cracking Down on Street Food After Poisoning
scenario: Municipal health inspector Nirmala Perera in Colombo is under pressure after a food poisoning outbreak linked to a roadside stall killed two people. Her superiors propose shutting down all unlicensed street vendors in the district. Thousands of families depend on that trade, and licensing fees are beyond many. The outbreak was linked to one stall's contaminated water. Nirmala must recommend how to respond.
options: Recommend closing all unlicensed vendors until they obtain permits, to prevent further outbreaks.
Recommend inspecting and closing only vendors found to breach hygiene standards, whatever their licence status.
Recommend subsidised licences and training for vendors, with temporary closure only for those who refuse to comply.

title: The Curfew on Teenagers After Knife Crime
scenario: Superintendent Callum Brodie in Glasgow is asked by local politicians to impose a dispersal order and informal curfew on under-eighteens in a district after a stabbing. Youth workers argue that it will criminalise teenagers who simply gather outside because their homes are crowded. Residents are frightened. Police data suggests that most violence involves a small number of known individuals. Callum must decide how to respond.
options: Impose the dispersal order and curfew across the district, accepting the burden on law-abiding teenagers.
Impose targeted measures against the small group known to be involved and leave other young people alone.
Increase patrols and youth outreach without any curfew, treating the order as too blunt and counterproductive.

title: Mandatory Flu Shots for Care Home Staff
scenario: Care home operator Esther Wanjiku in Mombasa is considering requiring all staff to be vaccinated against a seasonal virus that killed three residents last year. A few experienced staff, including a senior nurse, object on personal and religious grounds. Staffing is already tight, and losing them could harm care. Residents are frail and cannot be vaccinated effectively themselves. Esther must decide whether to make the rule mandatory.
options: Make vaccination mandatory with dismissal for refusals, since residents cannot protect themselves.
Offer vaccination as voluntary, but require masks and reassignment away from the frailest residents for the unvaccinated.
Make it mandatory with an exemption process for sincere religious objectors, who must follow stricter protective measures.
tension: protecting the vulnerable vs. bodily autonomy
religious freedom vs. duty of care

title: Ban on Night Fishing After Drownings
scenario: Fisheries and safety officer Iosefa Lemalu in Apia sees a rise in drownings among small-boat fishermen who go out at night without lights or radios. A proposed regulation would ban night fishing for boats lacking safety gear, but many cannot afford the equipment, and night fishing is the main source of income and food for coastal families. Iosefa must decide what to propose.
options: Propose a ban on night fishing for any vessel lacking basic safety gear, with strict enforcement.
Propose a subsidy programme for lights and radios, with no ban but a warning on risks.
Propose a ban only during forecast bad weather and strong swell, and allow fishing otherwise.
tension: preventing deaths vs. subsistence and liberty

title: Gated Access After a Landslide
scenario: Local official Esperanza Rojas in the Guatemalan highlands closes a road below an unstable slope after a landslide, putting a barrier across it. A group of coffee harvesters, who must cross the road each dawn to reach their plots before the harvest rots, demand to pass and have started to dismantle the barrier. Geologists say another slide is possible but cannot say when. Esperanza must decide whether to hold the barrier.
options: Hold the barrier firmly with police support, protecting people from a second slide.
Allow controlled crossing at set times, with a spotter on the slope and radio alarms.
Open the road and issue a clear warning, leaving the harvesters to decide for themselves.

title: Banning E-Scooters After a Pedestrian Death
scenario: City transport councillor Ingvild Haugen in Trondheim is pressed to ban rental e-scooters after a collision killed an elderly pedestrian. Scooter users, including many students and low-income workers, rely on them for cheap commuting. Data shows injuries are mostly to riders themselves, with a few to pedestrians. A ban would remove a transport option, but restrictions might be less effective. Ingvild must decide what to propose.
options: Propose a complete ban on rental e-scooters in the city, giving priority to pedestrian safety.
Propose speed limiters, pavement bans and licensed parking zones, retaining scooters under tighter control.
Propose no new rules but stronger enforcement of existing traffic laws and public safety campaigns.
tension: pedestrian safety vs. convenience and access

title: Fines for Ignoring the Heat Alert
scenario: Labour inspector Sunita Kapoor in Ahmedabad is told to enforce a new rule requiring construction sites to halt work from noon to 4 pm during extreme heat alerts. Contractors say deadlines will be missed and workers, paid by the day, lose income. Some workers say they prefer to work and rest in shade. Heat illness has killed several workers in recent years. Sunita must decide how strictly to enforce.
options: Enforce the noon stoppage strictly with fines for contractors, treating worker health as the priority.
Require shaded rest areas, water and mandatory breaks rather than a full stoppage, and inspect conditions.
Enforce the stoppage but require contractors to pay workers for the lost hours, accepting pushback.
tension: worker safety vs. income and choice

title: Evicting a Squatter from a Condemned Building
scenario: Municipal building inspector Gustavo Ferreira in Lisbon has condemned a crumbling 18th-century tenement. One resident, a seventy-year-old tailor named Joaquim, refuses to leave, saying he has nowhere to go and that he has lived there for 40 years. Inspectors say a partial collapse could happen at any time. The city has no free social housing right now. Gustavo must decide whether to proceed with removal.
options: Proceed with forced removal for safety and arrange temporary shelter, even if it is poor.
Allow Joaquim to stay in a reinforced ground-floor room while the building is propped, with daily inspections.
Delay removal until suitable alternative housing is found, accepting the building's risk in the meantime.

title: Naming a Contagious Neighbour
scenario: District health nurse Beatriz Quispe in the Bolivian Altiplano learns that a man in a small community has an infectious tuberculosis strain, but he has refused to take treatment because he fears losing his job and being shunned. Contacts include a school and a church choir. Public notification would break his confidentiality and could provoke social punishment. Quiet outreach might not reach everyone in time. Beatriz must decide how to proceed.
options: Inform the school and church contacts directly, prioritising protection of children and others.
Keep his name confidential and offer testing broadly to the community as a general health campaign.
Insist that he accept treatment or be placed on enforced isolation under public health law.

title: Capping the Crowd at the Pilgrimage
scenario: Pilgrimage safety coordinator Haji Abdullahi Musa in Kano state oversees an annual open-air religious gathering whose crowd has doubled in recent years. After a near-crush last year, engineers recommend capping attendance at 40,000 by pass. Pilgrims say that no believer may be turned away from a sacred duty. Enforcing a cap means turning away people who have travelled for days. Haji must decide how to proceed.
options: Enforce the cap with passes and turn away those without them, to prevent a crush.
Keep the gathering open to all but add more gates, marshals and staggered entry times to manage flow.
Spread the event over three days with time slots, asking pilgrims to choose a slot but not turning anyone away.

title: Cameras in the Apartment Stairwells
scenario: Residents' committee chair Mehmet Yıldız of a large apartment complex in Izmir proposes installing cameras in stairwells after burglaries and a fire that started in a hallway. Some tenants, including a woman who fled domestic abuse, fear being tracked and say recordings could be misused by neighbours or the management. Others want maximum protection. Mehmet must decide how to put it to a vote.
options: Propose cameras in all stairwells with recordings viewable only by police on request.
Propose cameras only at entrances and the basement, leaving stairwells unwatched to protect privacy.
Propose no cameras but better lighting, smoke detectors and a resident watch rota, accepting less deterrence.

title: No Alcohol in the Shelter
scenario: Shelter manager Thabo Molefe at a homeless shelter in Gaborone has a strict rule banning alcohol for the safety of residents. During a winter cold snap, a man known for drinking arrives intoxicated, and staff say that turning him out into freezing night could kill him. Others in the shelter, including recovering addicts, are anxious about his presence. Thabo must decide whether to apply the rule.
options: Apply the rule and refuse entry, protecting the other residents and the shelter's consistency.
Admit him to a separate room for the night under supervision, making a one-time exception due to the cold.
Drive him to the nearest hospital emergency room as a safe alternative, even if they may turn him away.
tension: rules protecting others vs. immediate safety

title: Warning Signs Versus Fences at the Waterfall
scenario: Park ranger supervisor Maya Cohen at a gorge reserve in the Negev must decide how to respond after a hiker died climbing past the warning signs at a high waterfall. The family wants a fence; many hikers and local guides oppose barriers in a natural place, saying adults should take their own risks. The reserve budget allows a fence or a new set of ranger patrols, not both. Maya must choose.
options: Install a fence and barriers at the most dangerous point, accepting the loss of unobstructed access.
Increase ranger patrols and staff briefings, leaving the area open with clear information about the risks.
Install only more prominent and informative signage and a voluntary registration scheme for hikers.

title: Mandatory Migration Out of a Sinking Island
scenario: Resettlement minister's aide Ioane Taetuna in Tuvalu is drafting guidance for the government's response to increasingly frequent king tides that flood the atoll's homes. Experts suggest compulsory relocation of the most vulnerable low-lying households to higher ground or abroad. Many families view leaving ancestral land as a loss of identity and refuse. Delay means repeated flooding and risk to health. Ioane must recommend a policy.
options: Recommend compulsory relocation for the most at-risk households, with compensation and cultural protections.
Recommend voluntary relocation with strong incentives and support, accepting that some will stay in danger.
Recommend investing in sea walls and raised housing on the island, keeping communities on their land for as long as possible.
tension: safety vs. cultural identity and autonomy
